ingredients.name: Strategy-tree walk (first-player coverage)
ingredients.what: Each relabelled iteration walks the net's own first-player tree (its raw move at its positions, every reply at the opponent's) and relabels those positions with the net's own search. The targeted coverage for perfect play from the start (P-START).
ingredients.conclusion: Works, and replaces the siblings for the P-START goal: perfect first-player play on 10/10 tic-tac-toe seeds with siblings off (h73), and on Connect-4 an iteration dropped from 4,008 s to 32 s together with parallel relabelling (h77).

ingredients.name: Solver-free stop signal
ingredients.what: Stop training when, on the net's own first-player tree, every raw move agrees with the net's own search (zero disagreements).
ingredients.conclusion: Safe and timely on tic-tac-toe with siblings (h69) and without (h74): 0 false stops, latency 0-1 iterations. On Connect-4 it never fires (h88). Most disagreements there are harmless — both moves optimal (59%) — or the search's fault (16%) (h90), but none of the nets is certified through 10 plies (h91) and at the first failing ply the net and its 200-sim search mostly agree on the losing move (h92): an agreement signal cannot be made safe on Connect-4 until the opening labels are right. Counting equal-value moves as agreement does not rescue it. A value-aware reading (a move also agrees within search Q 0.1 of the top move) passed the tic-tac-toe recalibration (h101), but only vacuously: it never differed from the share reading there (h102). On the six T10 Connect-4 nets it also equals the share reading at delta 0.05 and 0.1, and delta 0.2 removes at most 21% (h103, h105): the search itself values the rejected moves more than 0.1 lower, so the share rule already is a value rule. The value head is part of the cause but not all of it: it backs 42% of the nets' wrong moves (h106, inconclusive between the 40% and 60% bars), 57% at plies 0-4, and at the empty board every value head rates the winning centre below at least two other moves (h107). The rest are policy-side, where the value head ranks the right move higher one move ahead — yet the net's own 200-sim search labels an optimal move there only 47% of the time (h108, inconclusive), 15% at plies 2-4, and only 18% where the value head backs the error (h109). In the opening the training target itself is wrong at most of the nets' errors, so the value signal the search reads, not how the policy fits its labels, is the lever.

ingredients.name: Siblings (one- and two-move deviations)
ingredients.what: Relabel every position one (or two) moves away from the recorded self-play positions along moves self-play did not take.
ingredients.conclusion: Work on tic-tac-toe: one-ply siblings cut raw failures, mostly in-sample (h31, h38); two-deep siblings with augmentation gave raw-perfect nets on 10/10 seeds (h52), the remaining failures sitting on untrained positions (h57). Without augmentation they fail (h54, h55). They do not scale to Connect-4 (over 90% of an iteration, h76) and are replaced there by the strategy tree.

ingredients.name: Symmetry augmentation
ingredients.what: Train on every symmetric image of each example, with each game's symmetries found and verified rather than assumed.
ingredients.conclusion: Necessary in the tic-tac-toe process: every arm without it failed (h46, h50, h54, h55, h56), and augmentation with two-deep siblings gave 10/10 (h52). Convergence alone was not enough (h45). Symmetries are found by proof per game (t20).

ingredients.name: Standardised (canonical) input
ingredients.what: Map each position to its smallest-key symmetric image before the net sees it, so the net never has to learn the symmetry.
ingredients.conclusion: Shrinks what a net must represent (a 938-param net holds perfect tic-tac-toe when fitted to the answers, h51), but the solver-free process could not reach it at about 1K params, even with the final training pass matched to the oracle fit's budget (h58, h59, h60, h63, h64, h65).

ingredients.name: Relabelling with a deeper search (reanalyse)
ingredients.what: Relabel the whole buffer each iteration with a 200-sim search of the current net.
ingredients.conclusion: Works and replicates on tic-tac-toe, through the policy prior (h25, h26, h34, h35, h36, h37), but is a partial cause of the fix, not the whole of it (h28). On Connect-4 a 200-sim relabel search is silently wrong in the opening (h92), and more search does not fix it: 200 / 2,000 / 20,000 sims are right at 86.5 / 87.2 / 83.7% of opening positions and at only 33-60% of the first moves, 56% at 100,000 (h96; h93 inconclusive by its bars). The search reads the value head, so the value signal is the lever (stop_signal, h106-h109): value targets for the strategy-tree positions, from the relabel search's root value, do no harm on tic-tac-toe (h110: 10/10 seeds still perfect from the start, stop still safe). On Connect-4 neither they nor n-step bootstrapped value targets help: in a paired 4-seed pilot the share of optimal moves at the nets' own opening positions fell from 86% to 82% and 75% (h111, h112, both refuted). Both targets come from the net itself, and the readout shows the echo: with search-value targets the value head backs 73% of the opening errors, against 36% without (h113). A value target the net computes cannot add information it lacks; it has to come from real game outcomes. The backward curriculum (games started near the end, moving back) is the first such fix; it does no harm on tic-tac-toe (h114: 10/10 seeds still perfect from the start, stop safe), but in a paired 4-seed Connect-4 pilot it did not raise the share of optimal opening moves (72% vs 73%, 1 win of 4; h115 refuted). That pilot measure is noisy: the unchanged process scores 86% and 73% on two sets of four seeds, and single nets range from 62% to 94% (h116), so the three refutations rule out large gains only. The next pilot must be powered first. Scored on one fixed set of 5,142 exactly valued positions instead, nets of one arm spread 3.5 points and seed-matched differences 3.1, so 7 seed pairs detect a 3-point gain and 16 a 2-point one (h117); post hoc on that set all three refuted treatments read 1.7-2.1 points above base, a hypothesis that the powered pre-registered run (four arms, seven fresh seeds, Holm-corrected permutation tests) mostly did not reproduce: tree values -0.4 and the curriculum -2.3 points (h119, h120 refuted); only n-step kept its direction, +3.4 points on 5 of 7 pairs, uncorrected p 0.031, short of Holm's bar (h118 inconclusive; h121). No net in any arm is certified through 6 plies. Next real-outcome fix: an exploiter in self-play (the current net with 8x search, greedy, in half the games); its first tic-tac-toe no-harm run could not be judged because the run recorder missed the exploiter games (h122 not run; dead end h123, fixed); rerun on fresh seeds it does no harm (h124: 10/10 seeds still perfect from the start, stop safe); but on Connect-4 it changed nothing: +0.06 points on the fixed set (p 0.48; h125 inconclusive) and 71.1% vs 71.2% optimal at plies 0-4 (h126), though it played ~470 games per seed. Of the five fixes tried, only n-step shows a lead, and none makes the opening right (0 certified nets in every arm). Running the base process three times as long settles why: from iteration 20 to 60 general play keeps improving (+5.5 points on the fixed set, h128) but the opening does not move (+0.5 points at plies 0-4, h127 refuted; one seed fell from 75% to 68%). The opening is not waiting on a longer run — this self-play process does not learn it at this scale, whatever the value-signal fix. The hybrid's first measurement: an exact opening exception table computed by the process, with the net carrying the next ply, certifies on none of the ten nets at any horizon (h129, h130 refuted). The table overrides 50%, 26% and 15% of its positions before plies 3, 5 and 7, and the net is wrong at 23%, 12% and 12% of the ply it carries (h131): it improves with depth but its tree grows ~6x per ply. A hybrid certified through 10 would need ~190 table entries per net (~12% of its first-player positions). Training the net beside the table works: with self-play started at the table's frontier and the strategy tree walked from there, the net plays the optimal move at 81.6% of the 284 positions one ply past the table against 75.0% for the base process (+6.5 points, 6 of 7 seed pairs, p 0.016; h132 supported) and fails less at the never-trained ply 8 too (681 vs 865; h133). No hybrid certifies through 9 plies yet. Training the net on both plies it carries (6 and 8) from the frontier (H3) could not be judged: it was launched with 6 relabel workers against the registered 4 (h138; h134, h135 inconclusive by protocol). With the run's own worker count the registered tests are still inconclusive — +1.2 points at ply 8 (5 of 7, p 0.14) and a ply-6 curve that has flattened (+0.6 points over the last ten passes, most of the gain by pass 10; h139). H3 needs fewer table exceptions on 6 of 7 seeds (253 vs 278 entries; h141), but every certified-through-9 hybrid is over 25x the size of a table alone over the same tree: the 20,616-parameter net at 32 bits dominates, and break-even is about 1 bit per weight (h140). Through ply 9 the smallest certified description is the table. Priced properly — a complete table is one 3-bit move per first-player position in walk order, exceptions the cheaper of an index or a mask (h140 superseded) — the break-even precision roughly quadruples every two plies: ~0.2 bits per weight at depth 9, ~1 at 11, 3.7-4.35 at 13 (h144; the registered bar of 4 at depth 13 split, h143 inconclusive). The net stays wrong at ~9-11% of its own tree's positions even on plies it never trained (h145; the registered 2-point fall from ply 8 to 12 was not reached, h142 inconclusive). And the canonical table is not the smallest: the nets' own certified trees are up to 57% smaller, and against a table over such a tree break-even is ~1.3 bits (h146) — so the fair baseline is the smallest certified table, chosen to shrink its own tree.

ingredients.name: Unique buffer and final settle
ingredients.what: Keep each position once in the buffer and finish with a long, low-rate training pass (the settle).
ingredients.conclusion: Helps, not sufficient alone: with augmentation it was inconclusive (h49); a 1,500-epoch settle made the 5,008-param residual net raw-perfect where 30 epochs did not (h62 vs h61); it did not rescue the 1K standardised-input nets (h59, h60).

ingredients.name: Random openings
ingredients.what: Start self-play games after random opening moves to widen what self-play visits.
ingredients.conclusion: Does not work: mixed openings raised visits to the starved positions 4.5x without fixing them (h19, h20, h21, h23), so starvation is a correlate, not the cause (h22); six random opening moves failed in T5 with and without augmentation (h53, h56).

ingredients.name: Self-play search depth
ingredients.what: How many simulations the self-play search spends per move.
ingredients.conclusion: At matched compute shallow search first looked better (h3), but the effect decayed and reversed at full convergence: deeper search plateaus higher (h8). Part of the early gap was a deployment-budget confound (h9 holds at a neutral budget, h10 is null at the shallow arm's own). Deeper self-play alone did not fix the tic-tac-toe blind spot (h27), a failure of that recipe rather than of labels (h29).

ingredients.name: Exact solver labels
ingredients.what: Train on the solver's exact best moves instead of search labels (an oracle, not solver-free).
ingredients.conclusion: Without siblings, exact labels were the worst residual arm (h40): exact answers on the wrong positions do not give coverage.

ingredients.name: Net size and the smallest-net frontier
ingredients.what: How small a net can hold perfect play, and how the frontier is searched (oracle fits, strategy fits, bisection with checks above).
ingredients.conclusion: Tic-tac-toe: about 5K params hold perfect play (h47) and the process reaches it at 5,008 (h62). Connect-4 first-player play: 1,576 params certified through 8 plies (h67) and 20,616 through 10, with 8,008 unable to hold its data at 10 (h68, h72): roughly x5-13 per two plies. A 335K net trained earlier fails at its second move (h66).

ingredients.name: P-START certification
ingredients.what: The solver walks the net's own first-player tree against every reply and checks every move keeps the proven value (staged by depth).
ingredients.conclusion: Works as a staged certificate. The root value is taken as the theorem it is instead of solved (h78), the native solver's table bug is guarded (h79), and certified nets are now saved and independently re-checked (h87).

ingredients.name: Solver-free guarantee and parallel relabelling
ingredients.what: Proof that training called no solver, and the relabel search spread over worker processes bit-identically.
ingredients.conclusion: The unchanged process learned Othello with no solver (h1). The guard covers the Python and the native solver since h86. Parallel relabelling is part of the ~125x Connect-4 speed-up (h77); its result handoff no longer uses torch shared memory and a silent pool now raises (h89). DECISION 2026-10-02 (user): brute force (bigger nets, days of compute) and rules supplied from outside the process are ruled out. Self-play itself is NOT rejected: at our budget it plateaus wrong in the opening, 100x more labelling search, written certificates and a value-aware stop did not fix it (see stop_signal, search_budget, written_rules), and net size is not the limit (net_size), so the training method itself is the next suspect — first the value head's training signal.

ingredients.name: Written rules (§C.50)
ingredients.what: Play knowledge as logical statements (decision lists over predicates), verified exactly by the solver and fed to the other agents.
ingredients.conclusion: Win, block and fork are position-sound, and settle 89% of tic-tac-toe and 29% of the Connect-4 positions our nets visit (h70). Newell–Simon is a perfect strategy from the start for both sides but is not position-sound (h71). With only the 11 current predicates no position-sound playbook exists up to 12 rules (h94, pre-registered, refuted) or even 60 (h95): the obstruction is across positions, so the language needs richer predicates, not more rules. Adding three layered forced-outcome predicates (wins_in_5, gives_loss_in_4, gives_loss_in_6) makes a 3-rule, 3-literal playbook position-sound at all 4,520 positions, proven minimal by SAT (h97) — the knowledge moves into the predicates, whose lookahead (up to 6 plies) is the price. On Connect-4, Allis-style value certificates (a claimeven/baseinverse pairing for Black) never contradict the solver (h98), but they cannot supply the opening: none of the search's 144 wrong opening moves is flagged (h99, pre-registered, refuted). Through ply 8 of the nets' trees no position is certified, and certificates flag 0.5% of non-winning moves beyond the immediate-win tactic. They are an endgame tool, certifying 2 to 43 of 150 random positions as stones go from 20 to 38+ (h100). Discovered steady states (§3.6 S1): a generic priority-map rule (win; else the single safe move; else the first of 8 levels holding exactly one safe move), its content found by our own SAT search and verified twice (solver-free walk and certify), covers half the non-trivial positions at ply 14 of the exact table's frontier (25/50, h153 supported) and 19% at ply 12 (h156) — nothing within budget at plies 10-12 in the pilots (h152). Its value is bimodal: 11 of 25 states replace 12-432x their bits in table entries (85 bits play 12,229 first-player positions), the rest govern a handful of positions (median 5.7x, h154 inconclusive; h155). The search's time budget was soft (h157); it is now a hard deadline (h158). Complete certified strategies (S2): from each of 8 sampled ply-10 positions, table moves chosen to make children ready plus discovered steady-state leaves (a found map also covers a third of its non-trivial siblings) give a complete certified first-player strategy for the rest of the game within 28 minutes (8/8, h160) at a median 36x under the same strategy as a table (24-69x, h161): 18,219 bits play 250,840 first-player positions; pilot h159. What stops leaves at ply 10 is the search, not the language or a small budget: a 6x budget (30 min, 200K constraints) found a steady state for 1 of 8 ply-10 positions the pilot had left out (107 bits playing 6,115 positions; h162 inconclusive), and 14 levels instead of 8 found none — slower, not stronger (h163 refuted). Local search (WeakC4's proposal step) finds none of those ply-10 positions within 30 minutes (h166 refuted); its apparent 'one line short' (h167) was an artefact: the best map was the empty map, undefined at the root, and the score stopped at the first failure, so any map giving a root move looked worse (h170, superseding h167). Patching those maps with at most 100 exceptions gave no leaf (h168 refuted; h169 undecidable, h171). Charging a map for the whole leaf it makes — map bits plus the exceptions it needs on every line — fixes it: on the same 8 positions the search ends at a pure steady state for 4 (#705 in 23 s; SAT took 21 min) and at a verified, certified map-plus-exceptions leaf for the rest, median 39x under its table (2.5-159x; h172) and 260x under the empty map's leaf (h173). The score, not the language, was the ply-10 limit (h174). Handing those 4 leaves to SAT — started at local search's best map, its exception positions constrained first — finds nothing in 30 minutes and 200K constraints (h175 refuted), no more than SAT started cold (h176 refuted): the two arms do the same work within 6% (h177). Local search is the leaf engine at ply 10. From 4 ply-8 roots (S3, leaves from depth 4, SAT search, 4 h each), 2 strategies completed (h164 inconclusive): 647 positions in 205 bits and 318,473 in 34,115 bits, median 18.7x under their tables (h165); the other two ran out of time with ~400 of ~760 searches failing at up to 30 s each — the failed searches, not the tree, use the time. S4 reruns those 4 roots with size-scored local-search leaves that may carry exceptions: in pilots, accepting leaves at >= 4x completes a root in 31 minutes but leaves its bits over 90% exceptions (6.2x, h178); at >= 10x nothing completes within an hour, exceptions falling under 65% (h179). Registered at 10x and 4 h: 3 of 4 roots complete (h180; S3: 2) — #14026, which S3 could not finish, in 3.9 h: 657,615 positions in 99,451 bits — at a median 18.3x under their tables (h181). But where both complete S4 is not smaller: #3591 takes 64,047 bits against S3's 34,115 (h182 refuted), 78% of them exceptions. Size-scored leaves buy completion; their exceptions cost the size — as charged. Coded in walk order instead (a decoder replaying the leaf with the game's rules flags only contested positions — about 37% of a leaf's positions, of which ~1.5% carry an exception — knows undefined positions need one, and reads each move among the safe moves left), the exception bits fall by a median 59% (h183) and S4's #3591 takes 33,782 bits, no more than S3's 34,115 (h184); compression 34.7x and 31.7x. S5 lets leaves start at ply 10, two plies below the root: kept with exceptions at >= 10x the pilot strategy settles at 10.5x, its big leaves overlapping (h185); at >= 30x, 2 of 4 roots complete on a heavily shared machine (h186 inconclusive), median 20.3x (h187), and #3591 takes 24,908 bits for 295,930 positions — 35.6x, the smallest strategy for that root, over 20% under S3 and S4 (h189); #2071 is 10 bits larger than S4's (h188 refuted). Toward the whole game (W1, running): an opening from the empty board to ply 8 (label cache as oracle; the winning move whose replies the empty map most often wins) needs 204 moves and leaves 671 first-player positions to strategies; 8 sampled and built as S5 builds: 7 complete within 2 h (h190), each 33-49x under its own table — but the whole strategy projects to at least 7.97M bits, 12x the net and ~200x WeakC4, and ~415 h of builds (h191 refuted): three of the eight subtrees carry 86% of the bits (h192). The size is set by what the opening leaves, not by how each subtree compresses. Two cheap stand-ins to steer the opening by — unwon positions two plies down, and how soon the win can be forced — do not order the eight sizes (h193). P1 rebuilds the three largest with long searches near the frontier root (20 min at ply 8, 5 at ply 10): where they succeed the strategy shrinks five-fold — #323 4,304 bits against 25,324, playing 52K positions against 389K, since a map near the root changes which positions are reached — but the long searches starve the other two (54-56 searches against W1's 238-311; neither finished in 3 h), so both claims stay undecided (h194, h195; h196). P2 keeps only the root's long search (30 s below): #323 falls to 2,415 bits — a tenth of W1's — but #316 and #230 make only 16 searches each in 3 h, so neither claim is decided (h197, h198); profiling shows why — the leaf searches take over 95% of a build, and near the root one search step walks up to 450K positions and runs minutes past its budget (h200, superseding h199). Walks now honour the deadline, and builds share a map library; W2 redoes W1's projection with all of it: 6 of 8 complete (h201), every frontier strategy smaller than W1's — the three largest more than tenfold (#323 1,264 bits vs 25,324) — and the projection's lower bound falls from 7.97M to 533K bits, under the net's ~660K but not decided while two roots are unfinished (h202 inconclusive; h205, correcting h204); the shared library is barely used (2 of 61 leaves, h203 inconclusive) — the root searches carry the gain. W3 rebuilt W2's two unfinished positions for up to 6 h from W2's library: #316 finished at 9,057 bits, nearly tenfold its 2-hour partial, and #230 passed 5,446 bits unfinished (h206 inconclusive) — partials undercount badly — so the whole game projects to at least 1.62M bits, 2.5x the net (h207 refuted; h209), though ~5x under W1. For build speed, a C leaf walk returns exactly the Python walk's results but is only 2-7x faster warm and 1-3x cold — the exact solves bound it (h208); solving only the moves that decide (the map's move, else columns up to the lowest winning one) makes cold walks a median 6x faster again, results unchanged (h210). But rebuilding W3's two positions with the C walk (W4) leaves the build's time unchanged (#316 +1.4%) and #230 still unfinished (h211, h212 refuted): searches run to their budgets, so a faster walk becomes more evaluations, and the builds make fewer searches than W3's. CORRECTION (h216, superseding h213): P2-W4 registered budgets [[0, 1200]] — read by the builder as 20 minutes at EVERY depth, not 20 minutes at the root and 30 s below as described (P1's [[0, 1200], [2, 300]] likewise meant 5 minutes at every depth from ply 10) — so what P2-W4 call 'root searches' were 20-minute searches throughout, the build time was those searches' own budgets, and the root-only design was never run. Inside the C walk's wrapper, building exception keys took over a third of a walk (h215); built only when read, warm walks become ~16x faster again (h214). W5 ran the root-only design for real, budgets closed after the root, with the C walk: #362 became one pure steady state — 90 bits for 13,934 positions in 39 s (W2: 1,966 bits in 20 min) — but three first-wave builds overran the 2-hour cap by over an hour, because the builder's own Python walks ignored its deadline; W5 was stopped and its claims superseded (h220). The builder's walks now stop at its deadline and check maps with a C verify. W5b reran W5 with the fix: all 8 complete and certified within 2 h, the longest in 56 minutes (h221), in 30% of W2's total build time (9,562 s against 32,232; h223) — six of the eight are one map at the frontier root (90-470 bits), and #316 takes 6,675 bits in 35 minutes (W3: 9,057 in 4 h 21 min). Where W2 or W3 also finished, W5b's strategies are 44% smaller in total (7,766 bits against 13,842; h224). Yet the whole game projects to 2.42M bits, over W3's 1.62M lower bound (h222 refuted): #230, unfinished in W1-W4, completes for the first time at 21,054 bits — 73% of the sample's bits, 72% of them exceptions — where W3 had counted a 5,446-bit partial. One position sets the 8-root mean, so the projection is as uncertain as its tail. h221-h223 read post-hoc only because they were registered in the second the run started (t34). W6 built the next 32 sampled frontier positions as W5b (pre-registered): all 32 complete within 2 h (h225); the whole game projects to 4.31M bits, its 95% bootstrap interval 2.10M-6.85M all above the net's ~660K (h226); and the 4 largest carry 57% of the bits (h227). The frontier splits in two: 16 of 32 take under 200 bits — together under 1% — and the rest carry the size, 84% of all bits exceptions; the first 40 frontier positions project to 3.93M bits (h228). The opening cannot steer around the heavy positions at ply 6: 6 of the 13 decisions above them have one winning move, and every alternative at the others leaves 7 unwon replies, never fewer (h229). The builder keeps the first leaf with exceptions that clears its threshold, never comparing it with a split. A1 rebuilt four heavy positions with the threshold raised from 30x to 100x: all complete (h230), together 58% of W6's bits (h231) — exceptions fall to 7-31% of the bits, maps take their place — but the threshold cuts both ways: #594 falls 32,544 -> 6,207 bits while #565 grows 3,877 -> 18,093, its split reaching 7x the positions; the smaller build per position would be 39% of W6's (h232). The builder should choose leaf or split by size. A2 let the builder choose by size, building the split under every such leaf recursively: where it finished it beat both thresholds (#95 3,481 bits against 5,307; #535 6,637 against 12,857; three finished, 13,995 against 22,041), but it does not fit 2 hours — #565 kept W6's leaf when its split ran out of time and #594 did not finish (h233, h234 inconclusive; h235). The comparison must be made anytime: complete first, then improve. A3 makes it anytime — W6's build first, then the costliest leaves with exceptions split while time remains, each kept only if the strategy shrinks: all four complete (h236) in 16,740 bits, 23% of W6's and under the best fixed threshold per position (h237); each queue ran dry within 15 minutes of completion, the longest build 45 minutes, cutting each completed build by 54-82% (h239, correcting h238's slip). W7 rebuilt W6's 32 positions with the improvement (pre-registered): all complete (h240); the whole game projects to 1.47M bits, 34% of W6's 4.31M (h241), its 95% interval 0.78M-2.30M still above the net's ~660K (h242). Part of that is run-to-run variance — the same settings completed at 75% of W6's bits this time — and improving alone takes the projection from 3.25M to 1.47M; four positions kept no split, their only candidate a root leaf whose first split was larger (h243). Exceptions fell from 84% to 36% of the bits. A4 added lookahead — a split judged after its own leaves are improved — measured inside each build: it cuts what plain improvement left by a further 21% (37,848 -> 29,989 bits; h244) and unsticks both positions plain improvement could not change (h245); building and both passes cut the completed builds by 63%, every build done within 72 minutes of its 2-hour cap (h246). A5 spent the idle time re-searching the costliest leaves for 120 s each: a 0.56% further cut (h247 refuted, pre-registered) — only 29 leaves with exceptions were left to try, exceptions being 14% of the bits and maps 64% (h249). Maps are now most of a heavy position's bits, but they are not near-copies of one another: coded as edits of the map before, A4's 215 maps cost 18% more than coded whole (h248, a dead end). W8 rebuilt W6's 32 with the full pipeline (pre-registered): all complete (h250); lookahead cut 16% of what plain improvement left inside the builds (h253); the whole game still projects above the net (h252) — but at 1.57M, above W7's 1.47M (h251 refuted): the builds themselves completed 20% larger this run, a swing bigger than the pipeline's gain. Keeping the smaller of W7's and W8's certified strategy per position projects 1.26M (h254). Builder passes have run their course: the remaining cost is maps (58-64% of the bits), i.e. the leaf language. The leaf language next (user's choice). L1, maps of 4 levels at 2 bits instead of 8 at 3: 23 of 32 complete (h255 refuted) and at least 276,519 bits, 3.7x the 8-level runs (h256 refuted) — 2,132 maps against 586, larger on 25 of 32 positions: a map's expressiveness, not its cell cost, binds (h257, a dead end). L2 made the rule richer at the same bits — the first level holding any safe move decides, with its lowest move: all 32 complete (h258) in 14,666 bits, a fifth of the exact rule's runs (h259, both pre-registered), with 90 maps instead of 586; the whole game projects to 309K bits, its 95% interval 177K-469K entirely under the net's ~660K — the first projection below the net, on positions seen before (h260). W9 confirmed it on 32 fresh positions, pre-registered: all complete (h261) and the whole game projects to 271,740 bits, its 95% interval 137K-476K entirely below the net's ~660K (h262) — 12,908 bits over the 32, 104 maps, the builds 7.3 CPU-hours; the whole frontier would take ~153. WeakC4's ~35-45K is still ~7x smaller. More language (user's choice): L3 deepened what makes a move safe — not when the opponent can answer it with a forced win in two: all complete (h263) but 4.6% larger than L2 (h264 refuted) — it trades exceptions (34% -> 16% of the bits) for maps (90 -> 118), builds a fifth slower (h265). Maps are now most of the bits. Under L2's rule maps carry across the frontier in part: 35% of W9's fresh leaves are won from by a map L2 found elsewhere, none with exceptions (h266). W10 rebuilt W9's positions from that library (pre-registered): all complete (h267); the whole game, the library paid once, projects to 158,844 bits — 58% of W9's (h268); 13% of leaves use the library (h269 inconclusive). Most of the cut is one position (#638: 4,322 -> 356 bits, no library leaf), the rest 21% smaller: the library as a search start, covering, or variance — not separated (h270). F1 built the whole game (pre-registered): all 671 frontier positions certified complete under L2's rule (h271) — a certified first-player strategy for Connect-4 from the empty board in 548,424 bits (opening 1,075, seed library 8,618, positions 538,731), below the net's ~660K (h273) but twice W9's projection and above its 95% high of 476,290 (h272 refuted). The miss is sampling in a heavy tail, not drift: W9's 32 positions are light in F1 too (mean 342 bits against 803; 1.4% chance), the heaviest 10% of positions hold 58% of the bits, the median takes 154, and the seeded order's two halves cost the same (h274). The library carried little beyond the positions it was found on — 9.9% of leaves (h275). As a method, a 32-position bootstrap's 95% high fell below this frontier's true mean 11% of the time: projections from 32 positions are guesses, not bounds (h276). WeakC4's ~35-45K is ~13x smaller. The leaf language next (user's choice). L4 preferred forcing moves — of several safe moves, those leaving the opponent at most one reply that stops an immediate win, at no cost in bits — on F1's 16 heaviest and 16 spread positions against a control without it (pre-registered; a first run crashed on a coding bug before any evidence, h277/h278 superseded): only 4 of 32 complete within 2 hours (h279 refuted) and at least 160,659 bits against the control's 130,061 (h280 refuted) — a dead end. It starves the leaf search: maps found in 12% of searches against 44%, so builds run out of time splitting (171-201 table moves against at most 70), and where both complete it is never smaller (h281). The control — same rule, no library — rebuilds F1's 32 a tenth smaller (130,061 against 144,144; smaller on 20, larger on 12): run-to-run variance at the 10% scale, the library not needed (h282). Cheaper exact codes for the maps (user's choice), measured on F1's own 3,196 maps: the cheapest per map plus a selector saves 2.5% (h283 refuted, pre-registered); one code for all — levelled cells chosen among the empty ones — saves 3.2%, the selector costing more than switching gains (h284). Maps are near their information content under simple codes: their bits are set by how many maps and levelled cells there are. Another zero-bit rule (user's choice): L5 reads the safe moves on unlevelled cells as a last level, so a map needs level only what that default gets wrong. On L4's 32 positions all complete (h285) in 109,017 bits against the control's 130,061 — 0.84, short of the registered four fifths (h286 inconclusive) — but smaller on 24 of 32 (sign test p = 0.003), with 28% fewer levelled cells and 22% fewer map bits; the heaviest 16 take 0.80 of the control, the light 16 grow, mostly one position (h287). The first rule change since L2 that shrinks the strategies. F2 rebuilt the whole game with it, as F1 otherwise (user's choice, pre-registered): every position complete (h288) and a certified first-player strategy from the empty board in 455,959 bits — 0.83 of F1's 548,424, under the nine tenths registered (h289). Maps 24% and exceptions 21% smaller; F1's 67 heaviest positions take 0.72 of their bits, though the tail stays heavy (h290). WeakC4's ~35-45K is ~11x smaller. Longer searches on the heavy tail (user's choice): B1 gave the deeper leaf searches 120 s instead of 30 s on F2's 16 heaviest positions — all complete (h291) but 1.30 times a 30-s control's bits (h292 refuted, pre-registered). More time lets a search near the root clear the 30x acceptance threshold with thousands of exceptions: 9,094 against 1,972, while table moves fall 510 -> 196 (h293). The limit is what the builder accepts, not search time. Stricter acceptance (user's choice): A6 kept leaves with exceptions only at 100x on those positions — 15 of 16 complete (h294) but 1.34 times the 30-s control's bits (140,404 against 104,860; h295 refuted, pre-registered), smaller on 3 of 16. The bar cuts the first complete build to under half the control's (156,348 against 348,245 bits where both complete) but leaves the improvement pass less to choose from: improvement cuts the control's by 73% and A6's by 23%, so 3,436 bits of exceptions saved cost 17,814 more in maps and 21,166 more in table moves and leaves (h296). Which leaves to keep is best left to improvement, which compares sizes; the bar should stay low. Neither longer searches nor a stricter bar shrinks the heavy tail. Another zero-bit rule (user's choice) — first which: D1 sampled 4,523 own positions with several safe moves from L5's certified leaves and solved them. Ties go to the lowest move, which keeps the win at 93.2% (a random safe move 92.8%); no plain reordering does better (highest 93.0%, nearest the centre 91.9%, fewest stopping replies 92.3%), but preferring moves that win by force in two, then moves that do not lose by force in two ('tactics'), misses 200 positions against the lowest's 308 — 0.65, inside the two thirds pre-registered (h297). L6 builds L4's 32 positions breaking ties that way, against L5.

ingredients.name: Diagnosing failures (the tic-tac-toe blind spot)
ingredients.what: Where and why the nets fail: localisation, replication, starvation, the metric itself.
ingredients.conclusion: The blind spot is systematic and replicates (h11, h18, h24), is not explained by the eval budget (h12) or off-manifold enrichment (h14, h16), and self-play never trains the positions involved (h30). The coverage metric was wrong until it read every orientation (h39). Connect-4 accuracy away from training data is data-limited (h48).

ingredients.name: Training budget and game generality
ingredients.what: More games on the unchanged process, and new games without harness changes.
ingredients.conclusion: Returns past ~9,600 Othello games are unresolved (h2); the deeper-search arm was still improving at 28,800 games (h7). New games need zero harness changes (t7, t8). Kalah, the next ladder rung, plugs in as one file and matches the published solution (Irving, Donkers & Uiterwijk 2000) on every shape solved (h136); the paper's perfect games fit its stated rules best, its 4(6) line is misprinted (h137). Kalah's extra move is the first rule that keeps the same mover; the certifier, the search's proof step and the n-step target all assumed alternation and now compare movers (h148) — Checkers had avoided it by folding a multi-jump into one turn (t7) — with alternating-game training bit-for-bit unchanged (h147). Kalah is registered at the standard 6x4 and the exactly solvable 4x3 and 3x3, each shape under its own name. How small certified play is (E2): on every Kalah shape with a game graph of at least 1,000 positions, a certified first-player strategy decides at no more than 0.45% of them — Kalah(3,6)'s 1.57M-position game in 202 decisions (404 bits), Kalah(3,5)'s 767K in 74 (h149) — and choosing among value-keeping moves to minimise the tree at least halves the strategy on 7 of 9 shapes (Kalah(3,6): 2,699 -> 202; h150).

ingredients.name: Measurement integrity
ingredients.what: Resume, eras and fingerprints, the register, the statistics, mutation testing: the guards that keep results honest.
ingredients.conclusion: Each guard exists because an earlier reading was wrong without it, and each is a supported, test-backed claim; the two latest dead ends were a register hook that applied one arm's outcome to every arm (h82) and a hand-run mutation hidden by stale bytecode (h83). A pool deadlock voided 2.3 h of solving: one ProcessPoolExecutor.map over ~190,000 jobs blocked on Python 3.10's executor wake-up pipe (CPython gh-105829); exact solves now go in slices of at most 2,048 (h151). The same batch had passed once before — a race that passes is not evidence of safety. Runs stamp `started` in whole seconds, so a claim registered in the second its run started read as post-hoc (W5b's h221-h223); registering on data not produced yet now waits out that second (t34).

unproven_trials.what: The first Connect-4 depth-12 strategy run was replaced, with the user's agreement, by depth 10 with larger nets.
unproven_trials.lesson: Depth 12 costs days per width on this machine; get the depth-10 bracket first.

unproven_trials.what: The first depth-10 strategy run was stopped and restarted.
unproven_trials.lesson: Refits must warm-start and the label cache must be saved atomically after every batch, or a stopped run loses hours of solves.

unproven_trials.what: My mid-run reading of the depth-10 failures as loop instability was wrong.
unproven_trials.lesson: Read whether each refit held its data before blaming the loop (corrected in h68).

unproven_trials.what: An existing Connect-4 solver library (BitBully) was considered and rejected for its AGPL licence.
unproven_trials.lesson: Write our own solver (harness/c4solver.c, a port of harness/solver.py); the provenance of solver.py is still open.

unproven_trials.what: The C solver source could not join the code fingerprint, which parses Python only.
unproven_trials.lesson: The compiled library is named by the hash of its source, so an edited solver is always rebuilt and identifiable.

unproven_trials.what: A proof module was added to the evidence guard before its evidence existed, failing the suite.
unproven_trials.lesson: Add a proof module to the guard only once its data file is recorded.

unproven_trials.what: Changes to fingerprinted training code were needed while a long run was active.
unproven_trials.lesson: Work in a scratch copy and copy back after the run exits, merging the register and the evidence manifest rather than overwriting them.

unproven_trials.what: The first Connect-4 solver-free pilot (2-deep siblings) was abandoned after one iteration.
unproven_trials.lesson: Time one iteration before registering a long run (h76 records the numbers).

unproven_trials.what: Mutation specs and pilot data were kept in a temporary folder, and one spec was overwritten.
unproven_trials.lesson: Specs live in tests/mutations/ with their last run; pilot data goes to evidence/ and the register.

unproven_trials.what: Tried to reproduce Irving, Donkers & Uiterwijk's Table 3 game-graph sizes for small Kalah shapes: our reachable-state counts match for (1,1..6) and (2,1) but differ from (2,2) up (e.g. 22 vs 24, 58 vs 73, and 138 vs 58 at (2,5)); none of four rule readings (start-hole skip, non-empty capture, both, terminal nodes dropped) reproduces them.
unproven_trials.lesson: The table's counting convention is undocumented and its (2,5) entry looks doubtful; the paper's solved values (h136) and perfect games (h137) are the checks, not its graph sizes.
